summary: John's 5th-great-grandfather; Connecticut-born Pringle/Prindle who married Ensign Thomas Lamoreaux's daughter in Orange County, NY, and pioneered at Plymouth, PA, from the 1790s.
bio:
Samuel Pringle (often written Prindle) was born about 1767 (tree 1767-1847; one online tree says c.1770; WikiTree gives Monroe, Orange Co., NY, c.1767 without a record; FamilySearch says born in Connecticut). The Harvey Book says Samuel and James Pringle, 'brothers (presumably natives of Connecticut)', lived several years in Orange County, NY, before 1790, that the name was often written Prindle, that 'several of the name of Pringle and Prindle' were among the original purchasers of New Milford, CT, in 1703, and that the family descended from a Scottish emigrant. Round 3 rates Newtown/New Milford, Fairfield Co., CT as the probable home area. In Orange County a sibling group - David (m. Susannah Lamoreux 1783), James (m. Phebe Lamoreux 1785), Samuel (m. Martha 1790) and Hannah (m. Isaac Lamoreux 1790) - married four Lamoreuxs. FamilySearch (G99D-9DZ -> L8MP-W4X) makes Samuel a son of James Prindle (b. Newtown CT 5 Aug 1736; m. 22 Jan 1759 'Anar' [Hannah] Turner; d. Newtown 9 Nov 1800) with children James (c1754), David (1757), Benjamin (1764), Samuel (c1767) and Hannah (1773); The Prindle Genealogy (1906, p.41) confirms that James Prindle but lists no children, so this remains speculative. Round 2's suggestion that Benjamin Prindle, private in the 1st Regt, Orange Co. militia, was his father is downgraded: Benjamin now looks like a brother. Samuel married Martha Lamoreaux, eldest daughter of Thomas and Keturah, in 1790 (FamilySearch: at Smith's Clove, Orange Co.; an HSP marriage record image could not be opened). The Harvey Book says both families moved to Plymouth in 1794 (Thomas Lamoreaux himself moved in spring 1790 - conflict). A 'Samuel Prindle' is in the 1800 Plymouth census; he is on the 1796 assessment list and was Supervisor of Roads in 1800. He built a stone farmhouse near what became the Gaylord coal shaft; by 1873 'heaps of culm and stacks of machinery' had defaced it, and if the old farmer's spirit returned 'it is very doubtful... whether he could recognize the locality' (Wright p.391). An early Plymouth store's account books list him among regular customers buying 'rum, whisky, tobacco and snuff' (Wright p.308). He died 25 Mar 1847 in Kingston Twp (WikiTree; Harvey: 'March 1847') and is buried in Shupp's Cemetery, Larksville (FamilySearch). The Harvey Book says he and Martha had five sons (eight children in all); five are identified: Thomas (1791-1861), Benjamin (1794-1853), James (c.1799), Temperance (c.1802) and probably Samuel Jr. (m. Huldah Ives); John (m. Phoebe Davenport) is speculative.

The 1800 census of Plymouth Township lists 'James Prindle' and 'Samuel Prindle' one after the other, among the Lamoreaux, Steel, Van Loon and Davenport households ([R4-S1]). Samuel's household (a man and a woman aged 26-44, four boys and one girl under 10) matches him, Martha and their young family (Thomas b. 1791, Benjamin b. 1794 and others), and James's household is very probably his brother James who married Phebe Lamoreux in 1785. This is direct evidence that both brothers came from Orange County to Plymouth.

On Samuel's parentage, two primary records bear on the FamilySearch claim that he was a son of James Prindle of Newtown, Connecticut. The Newtown church register records that 'James Prindle & Anar Turner both of Newtown' married on 22 January 1759 ([R4-S2]), and the Barbour index card from Newtown Vital Records vol. 2 p.172 gives James Prindle's death as 9 December 1800 ([R4-S3]; FamilySearch and the 1906 Prindle Genealogy say 9 Nov). Samuel (c.1767) and Hannah (1773) could be children of that marriage, but the FamilySearch sibling list also includes James (b. c.1754) and David (b. 1757), who were born before the 1759 marriage and therefore cannot be Anar Turner's children ([R4-S4]). The FamilySearch family group is a reconstruction, not a documented family. Samuel's descent from James Prindle and Anar Turner stays speculative until a Newtown probate or deed record (James d. 1800) names him.
funFacts: His stone farmhouse was swallowed by culm heaps near the Gaylord shaft by 1873.
The store ledger shows his household's luxuries: rum, whisky, tobacco and snuff.

openQuestions: Parents: Newtown and New Milford, CT land and probate records for James Prindle (d. 1800) naming sons Samuel, James, David, Benjamin 'of Cornwall/Orange Co., NY'.
1790 vs 1794 arrival at Plymouth; Orange Co. (Cornwall, Monroe, Goshen) church and land records 1780-1794.
Newtown (CT) probate district file for James Prindle d. 9 Dec 1800 (Connecticut Wills and Probate, Ancestry; CSL probate packets): does it name Samuel 'of Luzerne County' or 'of Plymouth'?
Who was the James Prindle next door in 1800 (household with children up to 15, i.e. married by c.1785) - the James who married Phebe Lamoreux in 1785?

Prindles in the Hudson Valley before the move to Plymouth: a David Prindle lived at New Cornwall, Orange Co., in 1790, a few households from John Lomereaux and Oliver Davenport (1790 census, see Jean Lamoreaux I282695583838), and a Sgt. Moses Prindle served in Capt. Peter Harris's Dutchess Co. company in 1760 (NY Provincial Muster Rolls p.254). Check whether Samuel was in Orange Co. in the 1780s, before he married Martha Lamoreaux.

FamilySearch gives both Samuel Sr. (G99D-9DZ) and Samuel Jr. (KL4L-R8P) a death date of 25 Mar 1847, so one has been copied. No Samuel aged 70+ appears in the 1840 Plymouth Twp page that holds Benjn, Saml (30-40) and James Pringle; look for Samuel Sr. elsewhere in 1840 (Kingston Twp?).
